study.title: Isaiah 57 - Justice, idolatry, and the peace promised to the humble
study.overview: This chapter brings together three main movements. First, the death of the righteous is presented as something that the people could not discern, but that for them is a passage to peace, not defeat. Then the prophet denounces persistent idolatry, described with strong language of spiritual infidelity, violence and confidence in false support. Finally, the Lord declares that his answer to the humble is presence, healing, and peace, while the wicked remain restless and without peace. The chapter directly opposes two realities: the path of rebellion, which ends in void, and the path of contrition, which receives life and comfort from God.

outline.title: The death of the righteous and the rest in peace
outline.explanation: Isaiah regrets that the righteous perish without anyone realizing the meaning of it. The death of the faithful is not presented as the abandonment of God, but as an entrance into peace and rest for those who walk righteously. The text confronts the insensitivity of the people in the face of the loss of the righteous.

outline.title: Accusation against idolatry and spiritual infidelity
outline.explanation: The prophet calls the people to appear and denounce their corrupt spiritual identity: divination, adultery, mockery, idolatrous sacrifices, and alliances sought outside God. The repetition of bed language, nudity and travel shows the gravity of infidelity and the fruitless tiredness of relying on other powers.

outline.title: The Lord exposes sin, but promises healing to the humble
outline.explanation: God asks why the people forgot him, despite his prolonged silence. He declares that the apparent works do not profit, but also shows the way of restoration: the idols will be carried away by the wind, and whoever trusts in the Lord will inherit the earth. The holy God dwells high, but also with the contrite to revive and comfort.

outline.title: The wicked and the absence of peace
outline.explanation: The chapter closes with an image of instability: the wicked are compared to the agitated sea, unable to rest. The conclusion is solemn and summarized: the wicked have no peace, according to God Himself.

study.context: The notes provided show that the chapter was read in the context of the denunciation of idolatry in Israel and the comfort of the humble people. There is mention in the notes that the passage 57:13-21 promises the presence of the Lord with the humble and the restoration of his people, while he treats the ungodly. The idea that the death of the righteous is also appeared as part of the withdrawal of faithful from a perverse society, without this being the end of their hope.
study.theology: The chapter affirms a clear theology of the holiness and mercy of God. He is the Most High and Sublime, but does not remain far from the broken; on the contrary, he makes dwelling with the contrite to give life to the slaughtered. At the same time, God does not ignore sin: idolatry, greed and rebellion bring judgment, and no idol can save. The text also distinguishes between religious appearance and real trust in the Lord. Peace is not produced by empty rites, human covenants, or self-force; it is God's gift to those who humble themselves and trust in him. In contrast, the wicked remains restless because he has departed from the source of peace.

scholarViews.insight: The notes highlight that idols and other false support cannot help those who trust in them; the peace promised by God is worth the humble and contrite, not to the wicked.
The commentary presents the chapter as a sequence of observations on the death of the good, the idolatry of the people and the graceful return of God to restore their people.
The note understands the final verse as the exclusion of the wicked and unrepentant of all the promised peace before; they are outside the reconciliation and forgiveness given to the repentant.

questions: How do I react when one's fidelity to God ends in suffering or death: do I perceive it with faith or only with human sadness?
In which areas can I be seeking security in resources that I cannot save, rather than trust in the Lord?
What, in my life, needs contrition for me to experience the presence and healing of God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to abandon all false trust and to seek the Lord with humility. In practice, this involves examining whether there is idolatry disguised as prudence, reviewing priorities, repenting of persevered sin and valuing the peace that God gives, rather than chasing solutions that only tire the soul. It also encourages to comfort those slaughtered with the promise that God lives with the contrites and gives them alive.
study.uncertainty: The given text does not include notes for all verses, so the division of the chapter was made from the very flow of the biblical text and the few available observations. There is not sufficient basis, in the notes provided, to safely detail all the historical, geographical or political background of the practices mentioned. Some expressions of the biblical text seem interpretive translations; therefore, the analysis follows the general meaning presented in the passage itself and in the notes, without affirming technical meanings beyond what was explicitly indicated.
